hints: Recall that dissolving involves breaking the lattice apart and then hydrating the gaseous ions, so think how $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$ is built from those two steps.
Consider what happens to the sizes of the Group 2 cations down the group and how this affects attraction to the lattice anion versus attraction to water molecules.
If both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less exothermic, ask which one falls faster and how that makes the overall $\Delta H_{sol}$ more endothermic and less favourable.
walkthrough:
Link solubility to enthalpy of solution**
Think of dissolving as two steps. First you must pull the solid lattice apart into gaseous ions, which costs energy, then you let water surround the ions, which releases energy. The sum is $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$. If $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$ becomes more endothermic, dissolving takes in more heat and becomes less favourable, so less solid can dissolve.

Track both energies down the group**
Down Group 2, the cation $\text{M}^{2+}$ gets larger, from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. A larger ion has lower charge density, so it attracts both the large sulfate ion in the lattice and the water molecules in solution less strongly. That means breaking the lattice costs less energy and hydrating releases less energy. In other words, both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less exothermic.

Decide which effect wins**
The key is size match. The sulfate ion $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is very large, so changing the cation size has only a small effect on lattice energy. Water molecules are very small, so changing the cation size has a large effect on hydration energy. Hydration energy therefore falls more quickly than lattice energy, the balance shifts to more endothermic $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$, and solubility decreases.

Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group.
Both lattice energy and hydration energies become less exothermic down the group.
Hydration energy decreases to a greater extent than lattice energy, so $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$ becomes more endothermic and dissolving is less favourable.

hints: Start from the equilibrium $\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$ and remember which species is omitted from the $K_c$ expression for a dilute aqueous system.
walkthrough:
Write the water equilibrium correctly**
Water dissociates very slightly: $\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$. The equilibrium constant would include $[\text{H}_2\text{O}]$ in the denominator, but in dilute solution the concentration of water is effectively constant and is built into $K_w$. You are left with just the product of the two ion concentrations: $$K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]$$

hints: Recall whether ionisation of water is exothermic or endothermic and use Le Chatelier to predict what higher temperature does to $[\text{H}^+]$ and $[\text{OH}^-]$.
Think carefully about the difference between higher $[\text{H}^+]$ and being acidic, remembering that pure water always produces $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ in equal amounts.
walkthrough:
See why Kw rises with temperature**
Ionisation of water, $\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$, is endothermic. Heating pushes the equilibrium to the right, so both $[\text{H}^+]$ and $[\text{OH}^-]$ increase and $K_w$ increases.

Separate pH from acidity**
Since $[\text{H}^+]$ is larger, $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$ must decrease. Pure water at higher temperature has pH below 7, but it is still neutral because $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$ always for pure water. Equal increases keep the ratio $1:1$, so the ratio stays the same.

Final answer: pH: decrease
ratio $[\text{H}^+]:[\text{OH}^-]$: stay the same

hints: Convert pH back to $[\text{H}^+]$ using the inverse log relationship $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$.
At 298 K use $K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]$ and remember that $\text{NaOH}$ is fully dissociated so $[\text{NaOH}] = [\text{OH}^-]$.
walkthrough:
Find hydrogen ion concentration from pH**
You are given pH, so undo the log: $$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-13.25} = 5.62 \times 10^{-14} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ Keep the unrounded value in your calculator for the next step.

Use Kw to get hydroxide and link to NaOH**
At 298 K, $K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$. Rearrange: $$[\text{OH}^-] = \frac{K_w}{[\text{H}^+]} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{5.62 \times 10^{-14}} = 0.178 \approx 0.18 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, $\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ + \text{OH}^-$, fully dissociated, so solution concentration equals $[\text{OH}^-]$, $0.18 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

Final answer: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-13.25} = 5.62 \times 10^{-14} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$[\text{OH}^-] = K_w/[\text{H}^+] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} / 5.62 \times 10^{-14} = 0.18 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
concentration of $\text{NaOH} = 0.18 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$

hints: For added $\text{H}^+$, identify which buffer component can act as a base to mop it up and what weak acid it forms.
For added $\text{OH}^-$, identify which buffer component can act as an acid to neutralise it and what conjugate base plus water it forms.
walkthrough:
Show removal of added acid**
When acid enters blood, the base of the pair acts. Hydrogencarbonate accepts the proton to make the weak acid: $$\text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$$ This can also be written as forming $\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Because $\text{H}^+$ is locked up as weak undissociated acid, $[\text{H}^+]$ hardly changes.

Show removal of added alkali**
When alkali enters, the acid of the pair acts. Carbonic acid donates a proton to hydroxide: $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$ Hydroxide is removed as water, so $[\text{OH}^-]$ and hence pH hardly changes.

Final answer: $\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Write ethanoic acid reacting with water, with water accepting a proton to form $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and the acid losing a proton to form ethanoate.
Remember a Bronsted-Lowry acid donates $\text{H}^+$ and a base accepts $\text{H}^+$, so label each reactant and its corresponding product on the other side.
walkthrough:
Write the proton transfer equilibrium**
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, it only partly donates a proton to water: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

Pair them up as acid and base**
Going forward, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ donates $\text{H}^+$, so it is the acid, and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ accepts $\text{H}^+$, so it is the base. Going back, $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ donates $\text{H}^+$, so it is the acid, and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ accepts $\text{H}^+$, so it is the base. The two conjugate pairs are $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} / \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ / \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$
acid + base $\rightleftharpoons$ base + acid
$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ acid, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ base, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ base, $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ acid

hints: Calculate initial moles of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NaOH}$ using $n = cV$ with volumes in $\text{dm}^3$, and decide which is in excess.
Use the neutralisation $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ to find moles of acid left and moles of salt formed.
Convert the equilibrium moles to concentrations using the total volume $(30.0 + 20.0)\text{ cm}^3$, then set up $[\text{H}^+] = K_a \times [\text{acid}]/[\text{salt}]$.
Take $-\log[\text{H}^+]$ to get pH and round to one decimal place as requested.
walkthrough:
Find starting moles**
Work in $\text{dm}^3$: $$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.15 \times \frac{20.0}{1000} = 0.0030 \text{ mol}$$ $$n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})_{initial} = 0.25 \times \frac{30.0}{1000} = 0.0075 \text{ mol}$$ Acid is in excess, so all the $\text{OH}^-$ will be consumed to make salt.

Apply the neutralisation stoichiometry**
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Moles of salt formed equal moles of $\text{OH}^-$ used: $0.0030$ mol $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$. Moles of acid left: $$0.0075 - 0.0030 = 0.0045 \text{ mol}$$

Get equilibrium concentrations and hydrogen ion**
Total volume $= 50.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.050 \text{ dm}^3$. $$[\text{acid}] = \frac{0.0045}{0.050} = 0.090 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ $$[\text{salt}] = \frac{0.0030}{0.050} = 0.060 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ For a buffer: $$[\text{H}^+] = K_a \times \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]} = 1.75 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{0.090}{0.060} = 2.625 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ You can use moles directly in the ratio because volume cancels, but showing concentrations is safest.

Convert to pH**
$$\text{pH} = -\log(2.625 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.58 \approx 4.6$$ Give one decimal place as asked.

Final answer: moles $\text{NaOH} = 0.15 \times 20.0/1000 = 0.0030$; initial moles $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} = 0.25 \times 30.0/1000 = 0.0075$
moles $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ remaining $= 0.0045$; moles $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ formed $= 0.0030$
$[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] = 0.0045/0.050 = 0.090 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$; $[\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}] = 0.0030/0.050 = 0.060 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$[\text{H}^+] = 1.75 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.090/0.060 = 2.625 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$; $\text{pH} = 4.6$

hints: Look for the steep vertical fall on curve M and read the volume at the middle of that drop, where pH changes most rapidly.
walkthrough:
Read the middle of the vertical**
On reaction M the pH starts near 10.5 and falls slowly, then drops almost vertically from about pH 9 to pH 3. The end-point is the centre of that sharp fall. Reading across to the x-axis gives about $28 \text{ cm}^3$ of acid added.
Final answer: volume of acid added at the end-point $= 28 \text{ cm}^3$

hints: Estimate the pH range of the vertical sections for M (roughly pH 9 to 3) and for N (roughly pH 12 to 4) and compare with the table of indicator ranges.
Remember a suitable indicator must change colour entirely inside the steep part, so check which ranges fit inside each vertical drop.
walkthrough:
Match indicator range to the vertical**
For M the vertical spans roughly pH 9 down to pH 3. Both bromocresol green ($3.8-5.4$) and bromothymol blue ($6.0-7.6$) lie completely inside this drop, so either works. For N the vertical is much higher and longer, roughly pH 12 down to pH 4. Bromothymol blue ($6.0-7.6$) and thymolphthalein ($9.3-10.6$) both lie inside it, so either works for N.

State the selection rule**
An indicator is suitable only if its whole colour change interval falls within the steep end-point region. Then the colour changes with just one drop of titrant, giving a sharp end-point. Malachite green ($0.2-1.8$) is too low for both curves and would change too late.

Final answer: reaction M: bromothymol blue or bromocresol green; reaction N: bromothymol blue or thymolphthalein
Both indicators have a pH range of colour change within the vertical / sharp fall / end-point region of the graph.
